meta.title: Who really said "You have power over your mind - not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No translation of Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations contains this line. It’s a modern paraphrase of a genuinely Stoic idea — widely credited to him, but unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You have power over your mind - not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength'?
meta.ogDescription: No translation of the Meditations contains this line. It’s a modern paraphrase of a genuinely Stoic idea — credited to Marcus Aurelius, but unsourced.

answer.label: Not Marcus Aurelius’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The idea is authentically Stoic and at home in Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations, but this exact wording is not his. It appears in no standard translation of the Meditations and in none of Wikiquote’s sourced, disputed, or misattributed sections — it is a modern, anonymous paraphrase that quote sites (Goodreads, BrainyQuote and others) pinned to him. The nearest genuine passages say external things “reach not unto the soul” and that all disturbance comes from our own opinions within — the same thought, but never in these words.

source.excerpt: You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
trail: An investigation on Medium works through Books V and IV of the Meditations and concludes Marcus “likely never wrote this particular line,” calling it a victim of cumulative misattribution — Zachary G. Augustine, “You have power over your mind…” ↗.

A full public-domain English translation of the Meditations contains no “power over your mind,” “not outside events,” or “you will find strength” — the nearest lines speak of objects that “reach not unto the soul” (Project Gutenberg text) ↗.
Wikiquote’s Marcus Aurelius page ↗ catalogs his sourced quotations plus Disputed and Misattributed sections — and this line appears in none of them.
Quote sites nonetheless present it as his: Goodreads ↗ credits “Marcus Aurelius, Meditations,” while noting quotes are community-added and unverified.
source.excerptNote: The line as it circulates online. No translation of the Meditations renders any passage this way; the closest authentic sentiment is Book IV’s point that objects “stand without still and quiet, and…it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult…doth proceed.”
source.rightsNote: The ancient Greek text of the Meditations is long in the public domain, but this specific English sentence is not a passage from it — it is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author, translator, or first-publication date. With no traceable source work, no copyright status can honestly be assigned.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ruled Rome from 161 to 180 AD and is remembered as the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His private notebook, known as the Meditations, was written in Greek for his own use and never intended for publication; it became one of the foundational texts of Stoic philosophy. A recurring theme — that outer events cannot touch the mind, and that disturbance arises only from our own judgments — is exactly the idea this popular but unsourced line compresses.

cite.sourceCitation: Wording not found in any published translation of Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (2nd century AD); earliest documented as an anonymous modern paraphrase circulated on quotation sites. Nearest genuine sentiment: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV.

misattribution.heading: How the line spread
misattribution.intro: The wording is repeated verbatim across quotation databases and social media as Marcus Aurelius’s — but it traces to no edition of his work.

items.why: No published translation of the Meditations renders any passage as “You have power over your mind — not outside events…” A public-domain English text of the whole work contains none of its distinctive phrases (Project Gutenberg) ↗. It is a compressed modern restatement of a Stoic theme, not a translation.
As with many free-floating “wisdom” lines, it has occasionally been pinned to Einstein as well — a further sign it has no anchored source, as noted in the Medium investigation ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is genuinely Marcus Aurelius’s — his Meditations repeatedly argue that outer things cannot touch the soul and that disturbance comes only “from the opinion…which is within” (Book IV) ↗. The words, however, are a later paraphrase, not his.

context.heading: Why it rings true
lead: The line lands because it distills the core Stoic move: separate what you control (your own judgments) from what you don’t (everything outside). Marcus returns to this again and again — the “ruling part” of the mind is the one thing wholly in your power, and events are neutral until opinion gives them force.

That the sentiment is authentic is exactly why the misattribution sticks: readers recognize the Stoic melody and assume the specific lyrics must be his too. The sharper, more quotable phrasing, though, is the product of modern paraphrase, not of Marcus’s own pen — or of any translator’s.
context.pull: The thought is his. The sentence is not.
